title: From Recursion to Space Optimization
description: The universal four-stage journey every DP problem can follow, on one example

sections.title: 1. The Four Stages at a Glance
7. How to Approach Any DP This Way

blocks.text: Almost every dynamic programming problem can be solved by walking the same four stages, from a slow brute force recursion to a fast, memory-light solution. Learning this sequence gives you a repeatable path for any DP problem you meet.
We will evolve one example, Climbing Stairs, through all four stages. You can take exactly one step or two steps at a time, and you want to count the ways to reach step n.

blocks.caption: The same problem improves through four stages, from O(2^n) recursion to O(1) space

content.title: 1. The Four Stages at a Glance

blocks.text: Here is the whole journey before we walk it in code. Each stage is a small, mechanical step from the one before.

items: Stage 1, Recursion: write the natural recursive answer. Correct but exponential.
Stage 2, Memoization: add a cache. Now top-down and O(n).
Stage 3, Tabulation: remove recursion and fill a table bottom-up. Still O(n).
Stage 4, Space Optimization: keep only the recent cells. O(1) space.

blocks.text: The recurrence never changes across the four stages. Only the way we store and compute it does.
First, describe the answer recursively. To reach step n you either came from step n-1 or step n-2, so the ways to reach n is the sum of the ways to reach those two.
This is correct, and writing it proves our recurrence and base cases are right. But it recomputes the same subproblems endlessly, so it is far too slow.
We keep the exact same recursion and just add a cache. Each subproblem is now solved once.

codes.python:
def climb(n, memo):
    if n <= 2:
        return n
    if memo[n] != -1:                     # reuse the cached answer
        return memo[n]
    memo[n] = climb(n - 1, memo) + climb(n - 2, memo)
    return memo[n]

blocks.text: Time drops from exponential to O(n). We still use O(n) space for the cache and the recursion stack.
Now we drop recursion entirely and fill a table bottom-up, from the base cases up to n. The recurrence becomes a loop assignment.
Still O(n) time, but now there is no recursion, so no risk of a stack overflow on large n.
Finally, notice dp[i] only ever needs the previous two cells. We can throw the table away and keep two variables.
We started at O(2^n) time and ended at O(n) time with O(1) space, all from the same recurrence. That is the full DP journey on one problem.
Strip away the example and this is the recipe you can apply to any DP problem.

blocks.caption: Define the state, write the recurrence, add base cases, cache or tabulate, then trim space

items: Define the state: what inputs fully describe a subproblem?
Write the recurrence: how does a state combine smaller states?
Add base cases: the smallest states you can answer directly.
Make it fast: cache it (memoization) or fill a table (tabulation).
Trim space: keep only the recent cells the recurrence needs.

content.title: 7. How to Approach Any DP This Way

blocks.text: In an interview, you do not have to jump straight to the perfect solution. Walking these stages out loud is a strong signal and keeps you correct.

items: Start by stating the recursive idea and base cases, even if it is slow.
Add memoization to make it efficient and prove the recurrence.
Offer to convert to tabulation to remove recursion.
Point out the limited dependencies and reduce the space.
State the time and space at each stage so your progress is clear.

blocks.text: This sequence turns a scary blank page into five small, confident steps. It is the single most useful habit in dynamic programming.
